authoredPrompt: This figure pairs a flat structural drawing with a three-dimensional model of the same molecule, both cut by a horizontal plane. On the left, two carbons lettered "C" sit one above the other, joined by a vertical bond. The upper carbon bears an "H" above it on a dashed bond, an "HO" group at the left in magenta on a bold wedge, and a "CO2H" group at the right in green. The lower carbon repeats that arrangement flipped vertically: "HO" again at the left and "CO2H" at the right, but its "H" now points downward on a dashed bond. A pale blue parallelogram drawn edge-on slices horizontally between the two carbons, labeled "Symmetry plane". On the right the molecule appears as a ball-and-stick model, two dark gray carbons stacked vertically, each carrying a small blue sphere, a red oxygen with a second red sphere beyond it, and a branching green group, with an identical pale blue plane passing between them. Running the plane through both depictions asks the reader to check one half against the other. Because the halves are reflections, the molecule proves superimposable on its own mirror image despite having two chirality centers, the situation that defines a meso compound.
authoredInteractions:
- Click for selecting an HO, H, or CO2H group on one stereocenter; the reflected counterpart on the other stereocenter highlights across the plane, clarifying why the two halves cancel molecular handedness.
- Toggle between structure-only, model-only, and overlay views of the symmetry plane; the pale plane persists across representations, showing that the same internal reflection explains achirality despite two chirality centers.
authoredContext:
The 2R,3S and 2S,3R structures are identical because the molecule has a plane of symmetry and is therefore achiral. The symmetry plane cuts through the C2–C3 bond, making one half of the molecule a mirror image of the other half (the figure). Because of the plane of symmetry, the molecule is achiral, despite the fact that it has two chirality centers. Such compounds, which are achiral, yet contain chirality centers, are called meso compounds (me-zo). Thus, tartaric acid exists in three stereoisomeric forms: two enantiomers and one meso form.

A symmetry plane through the C2–C3 bond of meso-tartaric acid makes the molecule achiral.

The wedge-dash structure and ball-and-stick model of tartaric acid. C2 and C3 have a horizontal symmetry plane.

Some physical properties of the three stereoisomers are listed in the table. The (+)- and (−)-tartaric acids have identical melting points, solubilities, and densities, but they differ in the sign of their rotation of plane-polarized light. The meso isomer, by contrast, is diastereomeric with the (+) and (−) forms. It has no mirror-image relationship to (+)- and (−)-tartaric acids, is a different compound altogether, and thus has different physical properties.

discrepancies: The right ball-and-stick molecule is more flattened and schematic than the source, with less visible 3D depth and different substituent angles.
The pale blue symmetry planes are rendered as simple rectangular strips rather than the slanted parallelogram-like planes shown in the source.

The generated figure adds interactive highlighting/UI controls that are not part of the source visual, though they support the symmetry concept.
